metadata.title: The effects of vocational education on adult skills and wages (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses OECD PIAAC microdata (cross-sectional survey of adults aged 16–65) to compare adult outcomes by highest attained education type/level (vocational vs academic) at ISCED 3–4 and ISCED 5. The analytic sample is restricted to 17 countries with reliable identification of vocational vs academic pathways and further restricted by age (e.g., excluding those below 25; excluding 60–65 for labour-market and training outcomes due to retirement selection). The authors implement a multivalued treatment framework using IPWRA (inverse-probability weighting plus regression adjustment) with a multinomial logit treatment model and weighted outcome models; this is a weighting scheme for treatment-effect estimation rather than a stated complex-survey design weight variable (the manuscript does not report specific PIAAC weight variable names). Replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described in the provided text; standard errors are obtained via bootstrapping the IPWRA procedure (250 bootstrap replications).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a causal-treatment-effect report using PIAAC outcomes (earnings, employment, health, civic behaviour, training, and foundation-skill proficiency). The provided text does not describe a plausible-values (PV) workflow (e.g., Rubin’s rules across PVs) for the cognitive proficiency outcomes, and it also does not specify a general missing-data handling strategy for the full set of outcomes. While the report discusses missingness for PSTRE problem solving (including an appendix analysis using a missingness indicator), it does not document a comprehensive missing-data method for all outcomes, so the missing-data handling is treated as not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses PIAAC microdata and restricts to 17 countries where vocational vs academic distinctions at ISCED 3–4 are reasonably accurate in PIAAC. The sample excludes individuals aged below 25 (and excludes ages 60–65 for labour-market outcomes and continuing training due to retirement selection), while ages 60–65 are retained for analyses of proficiency in fundamentals skills and skill use. The main analysis focuses on individuals with at least ISCED 3 attainment; a final section additionally includes those with at most ISCED 2. The authors exclude education careers that are relatively uncommon in a country: if the share of a particular education career is below 5% in a country, they remove that treatment and corresponding observations for that country. For PSTRE problem solving, the report notes that problem solving is only assessed for respondents with sufficient ICT competence and who agree to a computer-based assessment; missing PSTRE proficiency is handled via an additional appendix analysis using a missingness/ICT-illiteracy indicator.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC adult survey data to estimate the effects of vocational education (VET) versus academic education across ISCED levels on adult skills and labour-market outcomes. The authors define four main alternative treatments (vocational vs academic at ISCED 3–4 and at ISCED 5) and estimate average treatment effects in a multivalued treatment framework using IPWRA (inverse-probability weighting plus regression adjustment) under a conditional independence assumption. The analytic sample comprises 72,769 adults aged 25–59 (with 60–65 retained for fundamentals-skill analyses) across 17 OECD countries where vocational/academic distinctions are reliable in PIAAC. Outcomes include hourly earnings, employment status, NEET/NET status, time spent in paid work, health, civic behaviour, training incidence/intensity, and PIAAC foundation-skill proficiency (literacy, numeracy, and PSTRE problem solving). Results show small advantages for vocational education at ISCED 3–4 in employment-related measures, but clear disadvantages for earnings and foundation skills at ISCED 5, with additional negative associations for health/civic behaviour and for ICT-related problem solving proficiency. The report emphasizes that causal interpretation depends on selection-on-observables assumptions and that missing-data handling is explicitly discussed for PSTRE but not comprehensively documented for all outcomes in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD report using PIAAC to estimate treatment effects with IPWRA (a causal inference econometric framework) rather than training machine-learning predictive models. The schema’s ML-specific fields (ml_techniques, main_findings as ML target rows) are therefore intentionally left empty, and confounders_identified is not populated because the report’s key controls are described as selection covariates within the treatment model rather than as ML predictors to be tabulated as conceptual confounders in this schema. The extraction is dense for methods and outcomes, but the schema’s ML-focused structure does not align with the report’s econometric treatment-effect design.
